message.content:
The ocean’s hue isn’t fixed—it shifts across a spectrum of blues, greens, and even browns or reds—depending largely on what’s happening below its surface:

| Factor | Typical Color |
|--------|---------------|
| **Depth & Clarity** | Deep, clear waters appear deep‑blue because longer wavelengths (red/orange) get absorbed while shorter ones (blue/green) scatter back out. In shallower areas where light penetrates less deeply, you’ll see lighter turquoise or greenish hues. |
| **Sun Angle / Time of Day** | At sunrise/sunset the sun’s lower angle casts warm tones over the horizon, turning the sea into pinks, oranges, or golds. Midday sunlight gives a crisp, bright azure look. |
| **Algae/Bloom Presence** | Phytoplankton blooms give the water a vivid green tint. Some cyanobacteria produce reddish-brown shades. |
| **Sediment/Turbidity** | Stormy seas stir up silt and clay, giving the water a muddy brown or gray appearance. Coastal zones near river mouths often show yellowish or orange tints from suspended sediments. |
| **Water Temperature** | Warmer tropical waters tend toward brighter turquoise or teal, whereas colder polar regions may reflect deeper indigo or navy blues. |
| **Atmospheric Conditions** | Overcast skies reduce contrast, making the sea seem duller or more muted. Clear skies enhance brightness and saturation. |

So when we think “the sea,” it could range from crystal‑clear cobalt at a calm beach to murky olive along a nutrient‑rich estuary—or anything in between!
